title: Fukanzazengi Part 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the fourth part of Eihei Dogen's Fukanzazengi, beginning with its detailed instructions for lotus posture, hands, and spine, and offering a gravity check for anyone leaning forward. Nomon tells the story of Argya Rinpoche, a Tibetan lama born to a nomadic family in 1950, who kept studying with his tutors while hauling manure on a Great Leap Forward farm, as a case that conditions for practice are always right. Nomon then sets the line "think of not thinking" beside a more literal rendering: "When a thought arises, bring it into spacious awareness... The self will naturally become whole." Nomon closes with Juan Ramón Jiménez's poem "I am not I."

sentences.text: Tonight I'd like to continue speaking about Eihei Dogen's text, Fukan Zazen-gi.
It's a universal recommendation for sitting meditation, for zazen.
You actually have the entire text in front of you.
It's very short.
So you could just listen, or if you're the kind of person where this is nice to do, you can look at the text too.
It starts on page 13.
It's like four little half-sized sheets long in English, about 600 characters in Chinese.
And this is the fourth talk on it, so it seems there must be some things to say.
And I won't quite finish tonight either.
Maybe next time I'll finish.
So Dogen is a very important ancestor.
Zen has a great emphasis on ancestors and the ancestral line, which comes largely from East Asian culture.
I'm sure they appreciated ancestors in India, but I think it was particularly emphasized once Buddhism came to China and to Japan.
There's a feeling in the air there that the ancestors are very present.
And we're such a new culture.
Most of our cultural forebears have not been on this continent very long at all.
Just a blink of an eye.
So they've been there for thousands of years.
So anyway, Dogen being an important ancestor, we study his texts.
He's also an unusual Zen master in that he wrote a lot.
And somehow, pretty much everything he wrote survived, which is kind of amazing if you think about it.
All these wooden temples in Japan were constantly burning down and being rebuilt.
And there were civil wars and foment and shoguns and samurai and all this crazy stuff going on from the 1220s and 30s into the 1240s when he wrote this stuff.
And now, somehow it all survived.
The very beginning of the text starts...
I made a big deal about this in the first talk.
The very beginning of the text, and you can see here if you want to look at it, doesn't talk about the problems of being a human being.
It doesn't talk about our problems that we might address with meditation.
Because we come here with problems, right?
We want something, some improvement or some help.
Or at least a nice way to spend the evening.
But the beginning of this text starts with an explication or an exploration of ways in which reality is actually already perfect.
The ways in which our lives, as they are, are actually just exactly what they need to be.
Even with problems, even with suffering, even with death happening in the illness.
Maybe we have noticed this more when the sun came out last Friday or wherever it was, you know what I mean?
It's like this sense of, oh...
It's not like Bellingham or Washington or the world is really that much different when the sun came out after that long, cold, wet spring.
There was a moment there of remembering.
Did you all experience that?
This is a wonderful place.
It's so easy for us to focus on what's broken.
It's not that that's not real in its way.
But the beginning of Dogen's text reminds us there's nothing wrong, there's nothing broken.
That's a warped and confused point of view that you bring here.
And you can let that go.
He says in here, everything is perfect.
The way is all pervading.
How could you fix that with your efforts?
How could you think that you could fix anything when we're so small?
*The whole body is far beyond the world's dust,* he says.
*Who could believe in a means to brush it clean?* Everything is just right where we need it.
So he starts there.
He brings up ancestors and then he goes on to talk about our attitude in practice.
And it gets very practical.
So this is the bottom of the first, no, the top of the second page.
Or the middle of the second page, excuse me.
He says for meditation you want to have a nice quiet room.
You want to be a little mindful about what you put in your body, in your mind.
And you want to settle yourself down.
And you want to stop this incredibly pervasive habit that we do so constantly that we don't even notice: dividing the world up into good and bad, right and wrong.
Me and them.
Him and her.
Male and female.
War and peace.
Everyone in these concepts has a sense of division.
They're provisionally true and provisionally useful.
You know, we can't really function without this.
But we're in some way caught by this constant dividing.
So they talk about dualism in Buddhism.
That's what they mean.
But he says that this sitting meditation is an opportunity to drop that.
To stop that.
And it takes quite a while.
We have to practice for a while to even notice how constantly we're doing that.
Sometimes when people first start meditation practice, they're a little bit surprised.
You would think that meditation would help you be calm or something.
But when you first start meditation, maybe some of you are just starting meditation, you might have noticed between 7 o'clock and 7:40 that things were not necessarily always calm.
Maybe they were calm.
Were they calm?
But there's a kind of foment in there.
You know what I mean?
There's a lot happening.
The mind is producing all these thoughts and concepts, and they're connecting and hooking and grabbing on.
The body is producing sensations, which is triggering more thoughts, which is triggering more sensations.
And it gets very gnarly in there.
And so Dogen is saying, there's nothing wrong with that.
There's nothing wrong with that.
There's nothing wrong with that.
Actually, remember, you're perfect.
But you could stop giving so much energy to this.
I want to do this right.
I don't want to do this wrong.
I need to try harder.
I'm not trying hard enough.
All these things.
So he says in the text, the way it's translated, *do not think good or bad.
Do not administer pros and cons.* Not only that, not only should you not indulge and energize those kinds of thoughts, but why not just cease all the movements of the conscious mind?
It's like, well, just stop, you know?
So how do you do that?
So that's where we ended the last talk.
So now you're all caught up.
So next is going to be very specific.
And this is the bottom of page 14, if you are looking at the text.
You don't have to.
He says, okay, well, here's how you do that.
*At the side of your regular sitting, spread out thick matting and place a cushion above it.
Sit either in the full lotus or the half lotus position.
In the full lotus position, you first place your right foot on your left thigh and your left foot on your right thigh.
In the half lotus, you simply press your left foot against your right thigh.
You should have your robes and belt loosely bound and arranged in order.
Then place your right hand on your left leg*
You're keeping it this straight, you know?
Right and left.
*Place your right hand on your left leg and your left palm facing upwards on your right palm, thumb tips touching.*
I'm always talking about this.
Oops.
Mudra.
Mine is backwards.
*Thus sit upright in correct bodily posture, neither inclining to the left nor the right, neither leaning forward nor backward.
Be sure your ears are on a plane with your shoulders and your nose in line with your navel.
Place your tongue*
It's very detailed.
*place your tongue against the front roof of your mouth with teeth and lips both shut.
Your eyes should always remain open and you should breathe gently through your nose.
Once you have adjusted your posture, take a deep breath, inhale and exhale.
Rock your body right and left and settle in to a steady, immobile sitting position.*
So he wrote it.
And I've looked at the characters for this and it's very literal and specific and it's exactly like it says in English as far as I can tell.
So this section confuses people a little bit when we chant this.
We chant this sometimes in ceremonies.
Because I notice not all of you are sitting in the full lotus posture.
The half lotus posture.
So it seems to be saying right away you're doing it wrong.
And there's nothing mentioned about chairs or seiza benches or support cushions.
And so one is tempted to maybe just strike this paragraph because it might make people feel inadequate, like they're not going to be able to do this.
That maybe it turns out, despite the fact that they seem kind of nice when we came in, actually this is like a very hard course or a spiritual athletic thing.
And if you're not up to snuff, you might as well walk.
And so it's tempting to strike it.
But the reason to leave it in, I think, is the message behind these particular details: it's really important to pay attention to the particulars of how you use the body to do this practice.
That it's actually an embodied practice.
And the details of how you set yourself up actually really matter.
And in our case, not being 20, 22-year-old Japanese men who sat on the floor as kids, we have to make a few adaptations.
We're working on this actually right now in the sangha.
The practice committee is trying to figure out what kind of information and trainings to offer.
And for each of us, it's a journey of discovery here.
What is the most stable, upright, balanced posture for this body, the way it is?
There's a balance there in terms of the quality of effort.

So we do want to make an effort to sit up a little straighter, be a little more open, to have the legs arranged in a way that supports that openness with the pelvis tilted forward, sitting carefully on the front of the cushion, planting the sits bones.
These things really matter because they create stability where you can really be still for 30 or 40 minutes.
They allow for openness and freedom of breath.
At the same time, each of us comes to this with our own crooked backs and arthritic joints and injuries and all of it, right?
So on the one hand, we're working towards opening into some posture, but we don't really know what that's going to look like for us.
And so there's a kind of engagement here with the body that actually matters.
And we don't talk about it that much.
We enjoy the Zen stories and the wonderful philosophies and the confusing, quirky teachings.
But not often do we really talk about the nuts and bolts of setting up the body and paying attention to the body.
But nor do we want to get too upset and wound up and uptight about it, because then we just get tense.
And that's something I've had a lot of trouble with in my practice, just like crying so hard to do it right.
So there is a kind of doing it right, and there's a letting go of doing it right, that coexist here.
And then some of this is very literal and practical, like this thing about leaning forward and backward.
That's really great.
So if you really set yourself up carefully on your cushion or on the chair so you're not leaning back, so you're upright, and you could try this now if you want.
Take an inhalation and extend the spine a little bit, visualize the spine coming up into the neck so that the upper body is a little bit longer but not strained, not forcing anything.
And then really being up and upright in both dimensions.
To do that, our mind is actually not that reliable.
If we can have the body extended and pivoting on the base of the spine, we can actually use gravity as a much truer sense of what is really up and down.

So if you just make little arcs from side to side and just let those be smaller and smaller, and are really attending and feeling gravity, you can just let balance and motion tell you what's up and down, what's left and right.
And looking around the room, you know, we're all a little skewed, left or right, forward and back.
Almost all of us are leaning forward a little bit, so you can also try the same thing, leaning forward and back.
Actual balance might feel to you like you're leaning back.
I think that's the case for me.
I think I've been leaning forward quite a bit lately.

And again, there's a balance here.
We want to allow the mind to settle as much as possible.
We want to release from this constant administering of pros and cons.

Let's just do a little gravity check here.
And yeah, sure enough, actual balance point.

More or less, you know, more or less.
Okay?
So Dogen says this, you know, in our 800-year-old text, very detailed: be careful about your posture.
It actually matters.
And the thing about the position of the legs, you know, it matters and it doesn't, you know, it matters and it doesn't.

It turns out the full lotus posture, just the way that the hips are rotated out, really makes a lot of space for the pelvis and allows some freedom there and allows this natural, you know, about 8 or 10 degree tilt forward of the pelvis, so that the spine makes this natural kind of S curve.

It's not the problem of the knees.
The knees are not the problem.

The body is a physical entity and these joints work in different ways and it's not too good to hurt your knees.

At the same time, one of the words that Dogen uses in here, which is always a little confusing to me, you might have noticed if you glanced at the book, he says right in the middle of the second page, *for sanzen, a quiet room is suitable.*
So what is a sanzen?
The term we use for sitting meditation is zazen.
*Za* means sit, and zen is zen, so sitting zen.
So why does he say sanzen?
That's bugged me for a long time, and I finally found out, and I've forgotten again.
*San* just means something like doing.
I'm going to have to look it up again.
I didn't bring my notes from the last talk.
It means something like doing zen, so for doing zen.
Or another way to look at this sanzen is: for zen that is just zen.
For doing the zen that is just zen is kind of what he means here.
I'm going to have to make one more talk again, so come next time.
But it means something like that.
Anyway, there's an incredible value, I think, in this very simple form where you just sit down.
You don't prepare.
You don't improve.
You don't spend ten years doing preparatory yoga practices to where you can sit perfectly in the full lotus.
You're not checking yourself: "Oh, I'm up to 23 minutes now.
Soon I'll be ready to go to Wednesday night.
A few more years, right?"
Instead, we just sit down.
We just sit down and let everything go.
The reason I think that's really valuable is that it's a great antidote to our tremendous smart powers of improvement and figuring things out and manipulation.
To just say, even though I don't really know how to do this, even though I'm confused by this, even though my posture is not up to snuff per Dogen, 12th century, I'm just going to do it.
I'm just going to sit.
I'm just going to breathe.
I'm just going to allow whatever my experience is to be my experience, without improvement, without adding anything, without manipulation.

That's part of why I think the Zen tradition has been resistant to very practical things like having warm-up exercises, because there's a tremendous spiritual benefit to engaging in something that's non-manipulative, that's not improvable, that is just being.
It's just being.
It helps us to disengage from this endless round of doing.
You know what I mean by that?
Do you think your to-do list is ever going to be done?
Does anyone think that still?
It won't, of course.
And we need our to-do list, but we have this glimmer that one day we'll finish our list, and it's really not true, and it makes us suffer.
This zen that is just zen, this sanzen that's just sitting, is an antidote to that, I think.
And strangely, very strangely, [unclear: "most confounds are doing mine"].
Strangely, and we have proven that here in a 20-year experiment.

We've done a 20-year uncontrolled experiment here with some people, and we had them sit zazen every week for 20 years, and they have all changed and grown in wondrous ways, even not knowing what the heck they were doing.
So it's now scientifically proven that something happens, even though you think, what would happen from doing nothing?
It doesn't make any sense.
There's a sense to it, a true sense beyond our usual manipulative sense.
Not to say you shouldn't take a yoga class, though.
Go ahead, go ahead.
Just don't think you're taking a yoga class to get good at yoga.
That would be a mistake, or to get good at Zen.
Do yoga just to do yoga.
And there's a sense, too, I think, in Dogen's text and in the style of practice, of not being caught by this very pervasive idea we have that we have to have the right conditions.
Things have to be right in our life before we can really take this on.
At the moment we're kind of busy, and we'll kind of try it, you know.
And later, after, fill in the blank: the kids are grown, I graduate, I have more time after I retire.
Later, later.
Conditions will be right.
Zen practice has a sense that these are the only conditions there are.
There are no other conditions.
So the only time to practice is now.
And that makes me think of Argya Rinpoche.
I don't know if any of you came when Argya Rinpoche was here.

So I want to tell you a little about Argya Rinpoche, because his talks brought up this theme of not waiting for the right conditions for practice.
I thought he was Mongolian, but it turns out he's Tibetan.

His family has Mongolian roots, but he was born and raised in Amdo province in Tibet, the same province where His Holiness the Dalai Lama grew up, although he was born a little later, in 1950, to a nomadic family.
So here's a guy sitting right here who was a nomad as a child.
It's amazing, the people you can meet who have gone through so many different lives and places and times.
We think of nomadic life as being thousands of years ago, but no. 1950.
Then when he was two years old, a strange thing happened, but a wonderful thing in their cultural context: he was recognized as a reincarnated Lama.
He's the seventh or eighth Argya Rinpoche.
So they have this whole system where certain Lamas have a lot of spiritual juju when they get reborn, to carry on their practice and their work.
I don't know how exactly new Lamas come into being.
It's a very complicated system, I'm sure.
He turned out to be a reincarnated Lama, and he told us about the systems of divination.
He said, I don't care if it was really him.
You can see movies and read books about this; it's really interesting.
It seems a little strange to us, but I think it actually makes complete sense from within the culture that it emerged from.
So, at two years old, or maybe three, he left the nomadic camp where he had been living and went off to live in this huge Tibetan monastery where monks live.
How many students are Western?
Okay.
So it's like a Western school, but a little bit smaller than Western only.
Everybody lives there and practices full time for seven years to life, not just four years of part time and partying on Friday.
So a little longer.
He says in the book that it was like he had a family of six thousand warm and loving family members.
It was great.
I think his mom came for a while, or his parents came and lived with him for a while, but then they left.
He was pretty young, but he was fine.
We find this very strange, taking a kid away from your family at four.
Piaget would not approve.

Then, a couple of years in, the Chinese invaded the country.
Right?
So he had to leave the monastery, and the young monks, at least, were all forced to go to school and learn Chinese and academic topics.
He says in the book (I don't remember if we talked about this in the talk) that he really liked it, actually.

So he really enjoyed learning Chinese and learning all his subjects.
And maybe he was too young to be horrified by the bigger political things happening in the background, as his country lost its sovereignty.
But then, after three or four years of that, when he was maybe about ten, Mao decided they needed to triple agricultural and industrial production in China.

All the monks were forced out of the schools and out of the remaining monasteries and onto these huge communal farms.
As you can imagine, Tibet is not a great place to have big communal farms, but they did it anyway.
So now Argya Rinpoche, at ten years old, is essentially a slave on a farm.

Hauling the manure and hoeing the fields, they continue to study the Dharma, and he was able to keep practicing.
A lucky thing, too, is that the memorization system came in handy, because they didn't have their books.

There are all these committees you have to be a part of, and re-education meetings you have to go to, and things you have to say and do and talk about.

And some of them got dragged.
You never knew if you were going to be shamed, embarrassed, promoted or killed.
You just didn't know.
So there was this unbelievable amount of uncertainty and unreality, you know what I mean?
In Bellingham, Washington, we have a fairly stable consensus reality, right?
We occasionally notice that we disagree, but basically we have a consensus about what reality is.
Not so in occupied Tibet.
You just don't know.
That happened eventually with the Panchen Lama.
He rose up the ranks, and then eventually he overstepped his bounds and got more or less repressed and marginalized.
